demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
try hard not think about the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Several selected items imply a hypervigilance/physical-assault style threat profile (scanning exits, reacting to sudden movements, avoiding open spaces) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one. These items usually fit interpersonal violence, combat, or other danger-based trauma more than bereavement trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Rehearse Conversations before any interaction' suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding threat or memory items about social humiliation, blame, or feared conversations about the death. It sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile and does not clearly connect to the active Memory→Threat→Strategies formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: These items imply a danger-based, assault-like or combat-like threat profile centered on physical attack and environmental vulnerability, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat content is internally coherent with hypervigilance for interpersonal/physical danger, but that pattern is not clinically well matched to the rest of the profile, where memory items reflect disorganized recall of a death-related trauma rather than threat from current spaces, exits, or others' movements.

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard' is more typical of interpersonal violence/combat threat cues and is hard to reconcile with a trauma of unexpected death of a loved one when the rest of the profile centers on grief-related memory disturbance rather than current danger from people.

vignette:
James is a 62-year-old stock broker who came to therapy on the recommendation of his physician after a routine check-up revealed dangerously elevated blood pressure. He had lost twenty pounds in the past two months and admitted he was sleeping only three or four hours a night. For a long time he had told himself he was fine, that his life was simply hard and he needed to push through, but something had shifted after a recent trading day when he found himself standing on the balcony of his firm’s thirty-second-floor office, gripping the railing and wondering whether it would be easier just to let go. He had no plan, he was quick to insist, but the image of himself leaning forward had scared him enough to make the appointment.

The event that had unhinged James happened eighteen months earlier, on a cold Tuesday in March. His younger brother Daniel, fifty-seven, had been driving home from his own accounting job when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection less than a mile from the house where they had grown up. James received the call from Daniel’s wife while he was still at his desk, watching bond yields climb. He remembered the precise second he heard the words — the digital clock on his monitor read 4:17 — but after that the memory fragmented. He could not recall driving to the hospital, or the conversation with the doctor, or even the moment he identified the body. What stayed were disjointed snapshots: the fluorescent hum of the hospital corridor, the cold metal of the chair he sat in for hours, the way his own reflection in the elevator mirrored back a face he did not recognize. He tried deliberately to reconstruct that night, to put the pieces in order, but the more he strained the more the images slipped away, leaving only that empty, buzzing feeling.

In the weeks and months that followed, James developed a set of habits that he considered common sense. He stopped listening to jazz because Daniel had been a drummer and every saxophone riff felt like a punch. He avoided the grocery store aisle where Daniel’s favorite brand of hot sauce was kept. When his sister called to reminisce about their childhood, he let the voicemail pile up until the inbox was full. The hardest thing to avoid was his own mind. For hours at his desk he would catch himself running the same loop: why had he not answered Daniel’s last text? Why had he canceled their usual Wednesday lunch because a client meeting ran long? The question — why did this happen to me, to us? — played over and over, a scratched record he could not lift the needle from. He tried to push these thoughts away by focusing on the market, squeezing his eyes shut and repeating stock symbols like a mantra. It worked for a few minutes, sometimes.

But the memories did not stay banished. They arrived as fragments, unbidden. The sound of a car horn on the street could suddenly throw him back into the hospital lobby, his brother’s wife’s hand gripping his arm, the antiseptic smell. His heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and for a dizzying moment he would be there again, not quite knowing where he was. These episodes came without warning and vanished just as quickly, leaving him disoriented and ashamed. He learned to scan his environment constantly — the hum of engines, the ring of a phone, the sight of a blue sedan like Daniel’s — so he could brace himself. At work, colleagues noticed he had become edgy, quick to snap, and unpredictably daring. He started making trades that were reckless even by his own standards: leveraged positions that could wipe out a quarter’s profit in an hour. When a junior analyst warned him against one bet, James snapped that the kid did not know what real risk looked like. He felt a perverse thrill in the danger, as if tempting something to punish him further. The guilt was a living thing inside his chest, and the risky behavior was the only way he could feel anything besides it.

His social world contracted. He had been divorced for ten years and had no daily contact with his grown daughter, who lived in another state. His few close friends stopped calling after he declined every dinner invitation, and his drinking crept upward — a glass of whiskey became three, then four, though he never considered it a problem because he never missed a trading day. The consequences of his avoidance accumulated quietly: his apartment grew stale and empty, his mail went unopened, and he found himself skipping holidays entirely, claiming he had to work.

What finally brought James to seek help was not the isolation or the drinking or even the weight loss. It was a moment two weeks before his physician’s appointment when a loud truck backfired while he was crossing the street. He dropped to his knees on the sidewalk, heart cannonading, convinced for an instant that he was back in the hospital corridor and the fluorescent lights were about to flicker out. A stranger helped him up, and James realized he could not remember the last time he had felt truly awake without the fog of a flashback or the grip of his own endless rumination. He was afraid of what he might do next, of the part of him that kept reaching for danger, and he was desperate to know whether the pieces of his life before the accident could ever be put back together.
